newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Air NZ alliance news imminent - Matthew.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Air NZ alliance news imminent - Matthew.

text.p: Air New Zealand Ltd is on the verge of making the first of what is likely to be a series of announcements on major global alliances, chairman Bob Matthew said in an interview on Wednesday.
"We are optimistic of putting in place significant alliance initiatives and the market won't have to wait too long for them," he said. "The work is largely done."
Speculation has been mounting that Air NZ and Ansett Australia, in which it recently acquired a half share, will make alliances with major airlines in North America, Asia and Europe.
The Sydney Morning Herald on Wednesday reported an alliance with United Airlines and Air NZ was possible and Matthew broadly hinted that such speculation may be accurate.
"Alliance partners are most likely to emerge from those markets where their strength adds something to us and that have a vested interest in this part of the world too," he said.

"A North American carrier with a strong position in North America, a relatively strong position trans-Atlantic, immediately comes to mind, as does someone based in Europe or Asia or both who gives us strong access to European markets."
Matthew, also chairman of Brierley Investments, which owns 42.5 percent of Air NZ, rejected selling part of its equity in a bid to secure any alliance.

"That's not on our agenda today. Alliances today have be based on the commercial merits. Buying shares in an airline doesn't give you any greater return necessarily than any other investor is going to get out of it. That, I suppose is the Qantas experience."

Qantas, the biggest competitor of both Air NZ and Ansett, holds 19.9 percent of Air NZ and there is speculation it will soon sell its stake. However, it took up its share of a recent rights issue that Air NZ made to fund the Ansett purchase.
Matthew said Qantas had given no advance notice of any intention to sell.

He said Air NZ would also be looking for alliances in Asia and Europe where access for Air NZ had been restricted. He declined to comment on media speculation that a partnership would also be forged with Singapore Airlines.

"There is no reason to make assumptions about Singapore Airlines but if you look on a global basis Air New Zealand will obviously look to create alliances in those markets and those routes where it is not strong itself," Matthew said.

"Most important to us, the mass of inbound tourism comes from Asia. North America and Europe are both important to us particularly since we have become an Australasian airline and because North America is a major market for Australia."
However, Matthew noted that the importance of various markets, particularly in Asia, shifted rapidly. He sees China as a potentially vast market and Indo-China as a "big play".
Matthew expects to see the gradual breakdown of bilateral air agreements, as is occuring in Australia and New Zealand.
"We are gradually seeing free skies emerge. I expect that ultimately the U.S. and Europe will agree on open skies. Old bilaterals will be over-ridden."
Medium sized airlines such as Air NZ-Ansett would have to have global partnerships to survive.
"I can envisage a day when we will be selling airline systems as distinct from brands -- combinations of three or four brands," Matthew said.
